subject: A histogram of the count of the count of a factor

messages.author: 42f6ac6cd9e82b3a
messages.subject: A histogram of the count of the count of a factor
parts:
I'm currently working with a rather large data set where I have one variable with 93 levels of a factor. My goal is to find a way to graph the count of the occurrences without needing to make a separate dataframe.  I mean, I could do that of course, but I'd like to find a way to accomplish the same thing within ggplot so that as I build more complex graphs, I can handle things as they come up. Let me try to explain what I'm talking about.

Suppose I have data like this:
df <- data.frame("Study" = sample(letters[1:10], 1000, TRUE))



Then what you might expect is that I would want to see Study on the x-axis and count on the y-axis, like this:
qplot(Study, data = df)



What I would actually like is to have (binned) count of Study on the y axis, and then a rather meta count of that count on the y-axis. I can get this by doing this:
qplot(as.vector(table(Study)), data = df)



But that's really inelegant and I feel like ggplot probably has some function that I'm overlooking.  I've tried various permutations of ..count.., but no matter what I do, if I try to attack it without summarizing the data outside of ggplot first, it fails.

Anyway, any guidance on this matter would be helpful!

Thanks,
Danielle

Elegance is great, but personally I'd take the slightly-less-perfect
solution (two steps, summarizing to an intermediate data frame and
then plotting) and move on to other things. This may or may not be
helpful advice, but consider...

Ben

messages.author: 42f6ac6cd9e82b3a
messages.subject: Re: A histogram of the count of the count of a factor
parts:
The only reason that I'd like to have something more elegant is because I have plans for expanding this to say something about the content as well through other layers and grouping.  This is the first foray into a series of probably 20 some odd graphs to present some summary statistics on a dozen cohorts that are all combined from other smaller cohorts.  Such a function would be really nice to have since I'm going to have to be very "meta-y" about the whole thing and this isn't just a one-off graph that I need.

Anyway, I totally get what you're saying, that sometimes doing things the simpler way is just the right course of action, but I figured I'd give it a shot just in case there was an easy solution I'd overlooked. 

Thanks!
Danielle
